topics.title: Application and Data Vulnerabilities and Attacks
topics.hook: A login form takes a username. Someone types characters that aren't a name at all, and the app hands back every user record. What went wrong in the code, conceptually?
concept: Applications fail when they trust input. In SQL injection, input is treated as part of a database command, letting an attacker read or change data they shouldn't. In cross-site scripting (XSS), an application includes user-supplied script in a page, so it runs in other users' browsers and can steal sessions or deface content.

Directory traversal abuses file paths (for example, sequences like ../) to read files outside the intended folder, such as configuration or password files. A buffer overflow writes more data into a memory buffer than it can hold, overwriting adjacent memory, which can crash the program or let an attacker run their own code.
All four share a root cause: the application doesn't properly validate or separate data from instructions.
terms: Injected script running in other users' browsers.
Manipulating file paths to access files outside allowed directories.
Writing past a buffer's bounds, corrupting memory.
Checking input matches expected type, length, and format.
traps: XSS runs in the victim's browser, not on the server's database. That's SQL injection.
Directory traversal is about file paths; SQL injection is about queries.

items.stem: Input typed into a search box is executed as part of a database query, returning all customer records. Which attack is this?
items.why: Input becoming database commands is SQL injection.

items.stem: A forum comment contains script that runs in every visitor's browser and steals their session cookie. Which attack is this?
items.why: Injected script executing in other users' browsers is XSS.

items.stem: A web request includes a file path with repeated ../ segments and returns the server's configuration file. This is:
items.why: Escaping the intended folder via path manipulation is directory traversal.

items.stem: A program copies a 500-character input into a space reserved for 64 characters, overwriting nearby memory. This creates a risk of:
opts: Buffer overflow leading to crashes or code execution
items.why: Exceeding buffer bounds is a buffer overflow.

items.stem: What root weakness do SQL injection, XSS, and directory traversal share?
opts: Trusting user input without proper validation or separation
items.why: All exploit unvalidated input.

items.stem: Which application flaw has the HIGHEST impact on confidentiality of an entire customer database?
opts: SQL injection in the login form
A typo on the About page
items.why: SQL injection can expose all database contents.

items.stem: Which attack MOST directly targets other users of a website rather than the server's data?
items.why: XSS executes in visitors' browsers.

items.stem: A code review finds user comments are displayed on pages without any filtering. How should this be documented?
opts: Vulnerability: stored XSS risk in the comments feature
items.why: Unfiltered user content rendered in pages is an XSS vulnerability.

topics.title: Protecting Applications and Data: Managerial Controls and Access Controls
topics.hook: A file shows permissions rwxr-x---. Who can read it, who can change it, and what single command would make it private to its owner?
concept: Access control decides who can do what. Role-based access control (RBAC) grants permissions by job role (all nurses can read charts). Rule-based access control (RuBAC) applies conditions (no access outside 7 a.m.–7 p.m.). Discretionary access control (DAC) lets the owner decide who gets access, like sharing your own file. Mandatory access control (MAC) uses labels (Secret, Top Secret) set by the system or administrators that owners can't override.

Linux permissions show read (r=4), write (w=2), execute (x=1) for three groups: owner (user), group, and others. rwxr-x--- means owner 7, group 5, others 0, numeric mode 750. chmod changes them: numeric (chmod 640 file) or symbolic (chmod g-w file, chmod o+r file, chmod u=rwx,go= file).
Managerial controls include data classification policies, least privilege (grant only what's needed), separation of duties, and regular access reviews.
terms: Access governed by rules/conditions such as time or location.
System-enforced labels and clearances; owners can't change.
Linux command to change file permissions.
r=4, w=2, x=1 summed per owner/group/others, e.g., 754.
u/g/o/a with +, -, = and r/w/x, e.g., g+w.
traps: In chmod, 'o' means others, not owner. Owner is 'u' (user).
777 gives everyone write access. It's almost never the right fix.

items.stem: In a hospital, all users with the 'Pharmacist' role can view prescriptions; doctors can also write them. Which model is this?
items.why: Permissions tied to job roles is role-based access control.

items.stem: What numeric mode corresponds to rw-r-----?
items.why: Owner rw=6, group r=4, others none=0 → 640.

items.stem: Which command removes write permission for the group, without changing anything else?
items.why: g = group, - removes, w = write.

items.stem: Documents labeled 'Top Secret' can be read only by users with matching clearance, and owners cannot change this. Which model applies?
items.why: System-enforced labels and clearances define MAC.

items.stem: Contractors can access the network only Monday–Friday, 8 a.m.–6 p.m. This is an example of:
items.why: Condition-based rules define RuBAC.

items.stem: A script file should be readable and executable by everyone but writable only by its owner. Which command is correct?
items.why: 7 (rwx) owner, 5 (r-x) group and others.

items.stem: A file holding private keys has permissions 644. What is the MAIN problem?
opts: Group and others can read it
items.why: 644 grants read to group and others; secrets should be 600.

items.stem: A user shares their own document with two classmates through the file's sharing settings. Which model is this?
items.why: The owner deciding access is discretionary access control.

topics.title: Protecting Stored Data with Cryptography
topics.hook: A laptop with 10,000 student records is stolen from a car. The disk is encrypted with AES-256. How worried should the school be, and what's the one thing that would change your answer?
concept: Encryption transforms plaintext into ciphertext using an algorithm and a key; decryption reverses it with the right key. Without the key, ciphertext should be useless. The keyspace is the number of possible keys; each extra bit doubles it, which is why longer keys resist brute force.

Symmetric encryption uses one shared secret key to encrypt and decrypt. It's fast and ideal for large amounts of stored data, such as full-disk or database encryption. AES (128, 192, or 256-bit keys) is the standard.

Block ciphers encrypt fixed-size chunks (AES uses 128-bit blocks); stream ciphers encrypt data a bit or byte at a time and suit real-time streams. The weak point of symmetric encryption is key management: anyone with the key can decrypt, so keys must be stored and shared securely.
terms: Secret value controlling encryption and decryption.
Total number of possible keys; 2^n for an n-bit key.
The same key encrypts and decrypts.
Advanced Encryption Standard, a symmetric block cipher.
Encrypts data continuously, bit or byte at a time.
traps: Encryption protects confidentiality, not availability: encrypted data can still be deleted.
A strong algorithm with a key taped to the laptop gives no protection.

items.stem: Which encryption type uses the SAME key to encrypt and decrypt?
items.why: Symmetric uses one shared key.

items.stem: Increasing a key from 128 bits to 129 bits has what effect on the keyspace?
items.why: Each added bit doubles the number of possible keys.

items.stem: Which algorithm is the standard choice for encrypting a laptop's entire disk?
items.why: AES is a fast symmetric cipher suited to bulk data.

items.stem: An encrypted laptop is stolen, but its decryption key was stored in a text file on the desktop. What is the result?
opts: The data is safe because AES is strong
items.why: Encryption is only as strong as its key protection.

items.stem: Which cipher type is BEST suited for encrypting a live voice call one byte at a time?
items.why: Stream ciphers encrypt continuous data as it flows.

items.stem: Why does a larger keyspace defend against brute force?
opts: The attacker must try vastly more possible keys
It removes the need for a key
items.why: Brute force time grows with the number of keys.

items.stem: What is the MAIN challenge of symmetric encryption when two parties are far apart?
opts: It is too slow for files
items.why: Key distribution is symmetric encryption's core problem.

items.stem: Which CIA property does disk encryption MOST directly protect if a laptop is stolen?
items.why: Encryption prevents unauthorized reading.

topics.title: Asymmetric Cryptography
topics.hook: You want a stranger to send you a secret, but you've never met and can't share a password. You publish one key to the whole world. How is the message still private?
concept: Asymmetric (public-key) cryptography uses a mathematically linked key pair. The public key can be shared with anyone; the private key is kept secret by its owner. Data encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the matching private key, so anyone can send the owner a confidential message.

The reverse direction proves identity: something encrypted (signed) with the private key can be verified with the public key, which is the basis of digital signatures. RSA relies on the difficulty of factoring large numbers; ECC (elliptic curve cryptography) achieves similar strength with much shorter keys, useful for phones and IoT.

Asymmetric encryption is slow, so real systems combine both: asymmetric cryptography securely exchanges a symmetric session key, then fast symmetric encryption (AES) protects the bulk data. HTTPS works this way.
terms: Shared openly; used to encrypt to the owner or verify their signature.
Kept secret; used to decrypt or sign.
Asymmetric algorithm based on factoring large numbers.
Asymmetric algorithm using elliptic curves; strong with short keys.
Proof of origin and integrity created with a private key.
traps: To send someone a secret, use THEIR public key, not your own.
If a private key leaks, the whole pair must be replaced.

items.stem: Bob wants to send Alice a confidential message using asymmetric encryption. Which key should he use to encrypt it?
items.why: Only Alice's private key can decrypt what's encrypted with her public key.

items.stem: Which key must NEVER be shared?
items.why: The private key's secrecy is what makes the system secure.

items.stem: Why do smartphones and IoT devices often use ECC instead of RSA?
opts: ECC gives comparable security with much shorter keys and less computation
items.why: Shorter keys mean less processing and power.

items.stem: HTTPS uses asymmetric cryptography at the start of a session and symmetric encryption after. Why?
opts: Asymmetric securely exchanges a session key; symmetric is faster for bulk data
Symmetric is more secure for key exchange
Asymmetric is faster for large files
items.why: Combining both gets secure key exchange and speed.

items.stem: Alice signs a document with her private key. How does Carol verify it came from Alice?
items.why: A signature made with a private key is verified with the matching public key.

items.stem: A web server's private key is stolen. What is the MOST serious consequence?
opts: Attackers could impersonate the server or decrypt protected traffic
items.why: Possession of the private key undermines confidentiality and identity.

items.stem: RSA's security depends on the difficulty of:
items.why: RSA relies on the hardness of integer factorization.

items.stem: What is the PRIMARY advantage of asymmetric over symmetric encryption?
opts: It solves the problem of sharing a secret key with strangers
items.why: Public keys can be shared openly, removing the key-distribution problem.

topics.title: Protecting Applications
topics.hook: Two developers build the same sign-up form. One adds security at the end, before launch. The other designs it in from day one. Whose app ships safer, and why?
concept: Secure by design means security is built into requirements and architecture from the start, not bolted on later. Secure by default means the product ships in its safest configuration: strong settings on, unnecessary features off, no default passwords.

Input sanitization and validation are the main defenses against injection attacks: check type, length, and format against an allow list; reject or escape control characters (special characters that change how input is interpreted, such as quotes, angle brackets, semicolons, and path separators); and use parameterized queries so input is always treated as data, never as commands.

Other practices: output encoding to stop XSS, safe memory handling and bounds checking to prevent buffer overflows, least privilege for the application's own accounts, keeping libraries patched, and code review and testing before release.
terms: Security built in from initial design.
Shipped in the most secure configuration.
Cleaning or rejecting dangerous characters in input.
Checking input matches expected type, length, format.
Characters that alter interpretation, such as ' " < > ; /
Query where input is bound as data, preventing SQL injection.
Escaping data before displaying it in a page.
traps: Client-side (browser) validation alone isn't security; attackers can bypass it. Validate on the server.
Allow lists (accept only known-good) beat block lists (reject known-bad).

items.stem: Which coding practice MOST directly prevents SQL injection?
items.why: Binding input as data stops it being executed as SQL.

items.stem: A router ships with remote admin disabled, no default password, and automatic updates on. This BEST illustrates:
items.why: Shipping in the safest configuration is secure by default.

items.stem: Why is validating input only in the browser insufficient?
opts: Attackers can bypass the browser and send requests directly
items.why: Client-side checks are easily skipped; the server must validate.

items.stem: An application should accept only 5-digit ZIP codes. Which approach is STRONGEST?
opts: Allow list: accept exactly five digits, reject anything else
items.why: Allow-list validation accepts only known-good input.

items.stem: Escaping characters like < and > before displaying user comments MOST directly prevents:
items.why: Output encoding keeps injected script from executing.

items.stem: A team adds security testing only in the final week before launch and finds a design flaw requiring a rewrite. What principle would have prevented this?
items.why: Building security in from the start catches design flaws early.

items.stem: A web app's database account has full admin rights though it only needs to read product data. Which principle is violated?
items.why: The app should have only the access it needs.

items.stem: Which pair of controls BEST protects a file-download feature from directory traversal?
opts: Validate requested filenames against an allow list and block path separators
Use HTTPS and a bigger disk
items.why: Restricting names and path characters keeps requests in the intended folder.

topics.title: Detecting Attacks on Data and Applications
topics.hook: A file's SHA-256 digest yesterday was 9f2c…; today it's 41ab…. Nobody approved a change. And a fake 'payroll' server nobody should touch just logged a login. What do these two clues tell you?
concept: Accounting means logging who did what and when: queries run, files accessed, records exported. These logs are the trail investigators follow.

Cryptographic hashes detect tampering: store a file's digest when it's known-good, recompute later, and any change, even one bit, produces a completely different digest. File integrity monitoring automates this.

A honeypot is a decoy system or file with no legitimate use; any interaction is suspicious by definition, giving high-confidence alerts and insight into attacker methods. Data loss prevention (DLP) tools inspect data leaving the organization (email, uploads, USB) and block or alert on sensitive content such as card numbers. Detection still has gaps: false negatives happen when an attack looks like normal use or slips past rules.
terms: Logging user actions for audit and investigation.
Fixed-length fingerprint of data; changes if the data changes.
Comparing current file hashes to known-good baselines.
Decoy system that attracts and records attackers.
Data loss prevention: detects or blocks sensitive data leaving.
A real attack that goes undetected.

compare.title: Tool vs. what it catches
rows: Attackers probing where no one should be

traps: Hashing detects changes; it doesn't prevent them or tell you who made them.
A honeypot isn't production. Real users should never touch it, which is why any touch matters.

items.stem: A configuration file's hash no longer matches its recorded baseline, and no change was approved. What does this MOST likely indicate?
opts: The file was modified without authorization
items.why: Any change to a file changes its hash.

items.stem: A decoy database server with no legitimate users records a login attempt. What is it?
items.why: A decoy built to attract attackers is a honeypot.

items.stem: Which tool would BEST detect an employee emailing a spreadsheet of customer card numbers to a personal account?
items.why: DLP inspects outbound data for sensitive content.

items.stem: Why do honeypot alerts usually have very few false positives?
opts: No legitimate user should ever interact with them
items.why: Since there's no normal use, nearly any activity is suspicious.

items.stem: Database accounting logs show a help-desk account exported 50,000 records at 02:00, far beyond its normal use. What should the analyst conclude?
opts: Possible compromised account or insider exfiltration
items.why: Abnormal volume and timing indicate likely exfiltration.

items.stem: An attacker slowly exfiltrates data by hiding it in normal-looking web traffic, and no alert fires. This is a:
items.why: A missed real attack is a false negative.

items.stem: To detect unauthorized changes to critical system files, which method is BEST?
opts: Regularly compare file hashes to known-good baselines
items.why: File integrity monitoring uses hash comparison.

items.stem: Recording which user accessed which records and when is called:
items.why: Logging user actions is accounting (the third A in AAA).
